{{use mdy dates|date=September 2024}}
A '''poll aggregator''' is an entity that tracks and aggregates individual polls conducted by different organizations in order to gauge public sentiment on key civic issues such as the approval rating of a major political figure (e.g., president, prime minister, monarch, governor, lawmaker, etc.), or legislative body; or to measure likely public support for an individual candidate or political party in an upcoming election.<ref name="AAPOR-Poll-Aggregators">{{cite web |title=Poll Aggregators |url=https://aapor.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/Poll-Aggregators-508.pdf |website=Am. Ass'n for Pub. Opinion Research (AAPOR) |access-date=13 February 2019}}</ref> 

== Individual poll aggregation ==
A poll aggregator may also forecast the likely outcome of upcoming elections by gathering and analysing pre-election [[Opinion poll|polls]] published by others, and/or utilizing other available politics-related information which, according to its methodology, may affect the outcome of an election. For example, an aggregator may attempt to predict the winner of a presidential election or the composition of a legislature, or it may focus on attempting to determine current opinion by smoothing out poll-to-poll variation.<ref name="Hillygus 2011">{{cite journal |last1=Hillygus |first1=D. S. |title=The Evolution of Election Polling in the United States |journal=Public Opinion Quarterly |date=1 December 2011 |volume=75 |issue=5 |pages=962–981 |doi=10.1093/poq/nfr054 |url=https://academic.oup.com/poq/article/75/5/962/1830219 |access-date=6 October 2024}}</ref> Editorial commentary by the site's owners and others complements the data.  Interest and web traffic peak during the last few weeks before the election.

How individual polls are aggregated varies from site to site.<ref name="Hillygus 2011" /> Some aggregators take a long- or short-term running/rolling average or average the polls at certain points in time, while other aggregators might take a weighted poll average (e.g., giving less weight to older polls), or use some other proprietary method of aggregation, based on such factors as past pollster accuracy, age of the poll, or other more subjective factors.  The averaging method has been criticized because it doesn't weight them by sample size.<ref name="Hillygus 2011" /><ref name="Linzer 2013">{{cite journal |last1=Linzer |first1=Drew A. |title=Dynamic Bayesian Forecasting of Presidential Elections in the States |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |date=March 2013 |volume=108 |issue=501 |pages=124–134 |doi=10.1080/01621459.2012.737735 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.2012.737735 |access-date=6 October 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>[https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB120303346890469991 "Election Handicappers Are Using Risky Tool: Mixed Poll Averages"], ''the Numbers Guy'', ''Wall Street Journal'', February 15, 2008</ref> In this way, the resulting average support percentages do not reflect the actual support percentage for any candidate of the pooled polls. According to the American Association for Public Opinion Research, "[o]ther aggregators use regression-based analyses — a method for adjusting data to account for unusual results ('outliers'). Other aggregators combine additional data like historical election results or economic data with current polling data through statistical methods – these are often called modelers."<ref name="AAPOR-Poll-Aggregators" />

Aggregators are not capable of accounting for systematic errors in the polls themselves. For instance, if pollsters are misjudging the turnout demographics, aggregators cannot undo these errors. Likewise, when there is a tendency to herd (i.e. for different pollsters to converge on a particular result to avoid being an outlier), aggregators will reflect this. However, veteran political journalist [[Bill Moyers]] has commented that poll aggregators are a good tool for sorting out the polls.<ref>[https://www.pbs.org/moyers/journal/10242008/profile3.html "Margins of Error. Poll Reading Tips"], ''Bill Moyers Journal'', October 24, 2008</ref>

[[RealClearPolitics]] was the first such website. It began aggregating polls in 2002 for the congressional elections that year. Several sites existed by 2004, including [[Andrew S. Tanenbaum]]'s [[Electoral-vote.com]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://electoral-vote.com/|title=Electoral-vote.com|website=electoral-vote.com}}</ref> as well as [[Sam Wang (neuroscientist)|Sam Wang]]'s Princeton Election Consortium.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://election.princeton.edu/|title=Princeton Election Consortium — Innovations in democracy since 2004}}</ref> Relative newcomer ''[[FiveThirtyEight]]'' began in 2008 by baseball statistician [[Nate Silver]], and continued under the name ''The Silver Bulletin'' after his departure from 538's owner [[ABC News (United States)|ABC]] in 2023.<ref name="Weprin 2023">{{cite news |last1=Weprin |first1=Alex |title=With Nate Silver Exiting, ABC News Finds Its Next Data Guru in G. Elliott Morris |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/digital/abc-news-finds-new-fivethirtyeight-chief-1235496339/ |access-date=7 October 2024 |work=The Hollywood Reporter |date=19 May 2023}}</ref><ref name="Silver Bulletin">{{cite web |last1=Silver |first1=Nate |title=Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential election forecast |url=https://www.natesilver.net/p/nate-silver-2024-president-election-polls-model |website=www.natesilver.net |access-date=7 October 2024 |language=en}}</ref> Pollster.com by Mark Blumenthal, was acquired by''[[HuffPost]]'' as Huffpost Pollster in 2010, but cut back in 2017.<ref name="Peters - 2010 NY Times">{{cite news |last1=Peters |first1=Jeremy W. |title=Huffington Post Buys Pollster |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/mediadecoder.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/07/07/huffington-post-buys-pollster/?src=twt&twt=mediadecodernyt |access-date=7 October 2024 |work=Media Decoder Blog |date=7 July 2010 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Wang 2017">{{cite web |last1=Wang |first1=Sam |title=Sharp cutbacks at HuffPost Pollster |url=https://election.princeton.edu/articles/sharp-cutbacks-at-huffpost-pollster/ |website=Princeton Election Consortium |access-date=7 October 2024 |language=en}}</ref> Since 2010, the political blog [[Talking Points Memo]] has also sponsored a "PollTracker" feature which aggregates opinion polls.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://polltracker.talkingpointsmemo.com/ |title=TPM PollTracker |access-date=2011-05-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110513014443/http://polltracker.talkingpointsmemo.com/ |archive-date=2011-05-13 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Other noteworthy examples include [[Drew Linzer]]'s Votamatic,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://votamatic.org/|title=VOTAMATIC|website=VOTAMATIC}}</ref> Josh Putnam's Frontloading HQ,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.frontloadinghq.com/|title=Frontloading HQ}}</ref> and Jay DeSart and Tom Holbrook's Politics by the Numbers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://politics-by-the-numbers.blogspot.de/|title=Politics by the Numbers|website=politics-by-the-numbers.blogspot.de}}</ref> In Australia, William Bowe's Poll Bludger hosts the BludgerTrack poll aggregator. [[Europe Elects]], founded in 2014, is another poll aggregator that collects voting intention polling data from across the European continent. An example of aggregator of poll aggregators includes the [[PollyVote]], which combines different polling averages as one component of a combined forecast of the U.S. presidential election result.<ref name="GraefeetalPS">{{cite journal|last=Graefe|first=Andreas |author2=Armstrong, J. Scott |author3=Jones, Randall J. Jr |author4=and Alfred G. Cuzán |title=Accuracy of combined forecasts for the 2012 Presidential Elections: The PollyVote|journal=PS: Political Science & Politics|year=2014|volume=47|issue=2|pages=427–431|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237050409|publisher=Cambridge Journals |doi=10.1017/s1049096514000341|s2cid=53974907 }}</ref>
